objectives.text: Explain and interpret energy changes in chemical reactions.

lesson.title: Understanding Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions
lesson.summary: This lesson explains exothermic and endothermic reactions using energy profiles and numerical data. It helps learners distinguish between energy transfer and temperature changes while interpreting simple chemical energy diagrams.

objectives.text: Explain and interpret energy changes in chemical reactions.

sections.heading: Defining Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions
sections.body: Exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings, causing a temperature rise. Endothermic reactions absorb energy from the surroundings, leading to a temperature drop. Understanding these definitions helps you predict how a reaction will feel and how energy moves between the system and its environment during chemical changes.

sections.heading: Interpreting Energy Profile Diagrams
sections.body: Energy profiles show the energy levels of reactants and products. The vertical axis represents energy, while the horizontal axis shows the reaction progress. A lower product energy level indicates an exothermic reaction. A higher product energy level indicates an endothermic reaction. The difference between these levels equals the energy change.

sections.heading: Distinguishing Energy Transfer from Temperature
sections.body: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of particles, while energy transfer is the total heat moved. A small mass can show a large temperature change with little total energy transfer. Always calculate total energy using mass and specific heat capacity. Do not confuse a hot cup of tea with a swimming pool regarding total energy content.

practice.prompt: A reaction releases 500 J of energy to the surroundings. The reactants start at 25°C. Which statement correctly describes this reaction?
options: It is endothermic because the temperature is high.
It is exothermic because energy leaves the system.
It is endothermic because energy is released.
It is exothermic because the temperature increases.
practice.explanation: Releasing energy to the surroundings defines an exothermic reaction, regardless of the starting temperature.

practice.prompt: An energy profile shows reactants at 100 kJ and products at 150 kJ. What is the energy change for this reaction?
options: 250 kJ, indicating a large exothermic release.
practice.explanation: Products having higher energy than reactants means energy was absorbed, making the change positive and endothermic.

practice.prompt: A 10 g sample heats up by 5°C. A 1000 g sample heats up by 0.5°C. Which sample likely transferred more total energy?
options: The 10 g sample because its temperature change is larger.
The 1000 g sample because its mass is significantly larger.
Both samples transferred exactly the same amount of energy.
Neither sample transferred any measurable energy.
practice.explanation: Total energy transfer depends on mass and temperature change; the larger mass generally implies greater total energy despite the smaller temperature rise.
